reconcile.connective: Matthew Henry insists the lily saying forbids anxious care, not the ordinary labor and thrift Scripture elsewhere commends — idleness, not providence, tempts God.

discrepancy.connective: Sociologist Gerd Theissen documents a real shift: Jesus's itinerant, possessionless ethic later gave way to the settled household norms 1 Timothy enforces.

skeptic.name: Gerd Theissen
skeptic.attribution: Gerd Theissen, Sociology of Early Palestinian Christianity (Fortress Press, 1978; German original Soziologie der Jesusbewegung, 1977)

excerpts.excerpt_text: It does not follow that we must therefore neglect, or do carelessly, the proper business of this life; it is the praise of the virtuous woman, that she lays her hand to the spindle, makes fine linen and sells it, Pro 31:19, Pro 31:24. Idleness tempts God, instead of trusting him; but he that provides for inferior creatures, without their labour, will much more provide for us, by blessing our labour, which he has made our duty.
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly denies that 'consider the lilies' licenses neglect of ordinary labor or providing, tying industriousness (echoing the Proverbs 31 virtuous woman) to trust rather than opposing it — the crux of the improvidence charge.

pd_work.resource: John W. Haley, An Examination of the Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible (1874)
pd_work.author: John W. Haley
pd_work.note: Haley treats this exact contradiction under the heading 'Improvidence,' pairing Matt 6:19,25,34 and Luke 6:30/12:33 against Prov 13:22 and 1 Tim 5:8, and argues 'take no thought' means freedom from anxious solicitude, not license for wastefulness (pp. 280-281).
